sheet-1.description: The lower two thirds of the index sheet, drawn at 100 ft to an inch, covering the south-western corner of Little Ferry along the boundary with the Borough of Moonachie. Liberty Street crosses the top of the map from the north-east and turns west towards Moonachie, where a short stub is lettered Moonachie St. Eckel Road runs south from Liberty through the western blocks, crossed by Adams, Jefferson, Madison and Monroe Streets, laid out as narrow building lots that are mostly still vacant; only Adams Street and Eckel Road carry a scattering of one- and two-storey frame dwellings. The Riser Drainage Ditch and the borough limit run diagonally along the west side, beyond which the Moonachie ground is left blank with a reference to the Garfield volume. The eastern half shows a more built-up grid between Hester Street and Mehrhof Road: Warren Street with the end of Nicholas Avenue, Henches Place, Coomann Street and Columbus Avenue, lined with frame dwellings, a few concrete-block garages, a brick-cased house and a small printing shop on Columbus Avenue. Short stubs of Hartwick, Lafayette and Lincoln Streets lead east off Mehrhof Road towards sheet 6. Large open tracts (blocks 55, 78 and 80) separate the two halves. The sheet also carries the map key, a New Jersey location map (outside the georeferenced area), the scale bar and a compass rose; the upper third of the page holds the index, key map and water and fire department notes and is not part of this part.
notes: Liberty Street west of Eckel Road is now Moonachie Road.
Coomann Street is now Prospect Avenue.
Nicholas Avenue is now Nicholas Street.
The Moonachie side of the borough line is left blank: 'See Garfield Volume'.
Modern Columbus Avenue continues west to Madison Street; in 1925 it ended in the open block west of Hester Street.
Eckel Road / Jefferson Street was rejected by the fit (18 m), and Hester Street / Prospect Avenue (6.7 m): Jefferson Street and Prospect Avenue appear realigned at these corners.

Map, 100 ft. Upper third is the index, key map (1200 ft to an inch), title cartouche and water/fire notes; not georeferenced. Lower two thirds is a 100 ft map of the south-west of the borough: Liberty (now Moonachie Road west of Eckel), Eckel Rd, Adams, Jefferson, Madison, Monroe, Hester, Warren, Nicholas Av, Henches Pl, Coomann (now Prospect Avenue), Columbus Av, Mehrhof Rd. One configured part (config sheet-1, mask below the double rule, New Jersey location inset notched out).

sheet-2.description: The centre of Little Ferry at 100 ft to an inch, between the Moonachie borough line on the west and Mehrhof Road on the east. Liberty Street curves through the middle of the sheet from Kavrik and William Streets in the north to its meeting with Eckel Road in the south, and Washington Avenue runs east from Liberty to Mehrhof Road. West of Liberty lie Niehaus Avenue and Union Avenue, crossed by Henry, Christina and Sabina Streets, with the northern ends of Charles and Jackson Streets beyond; the Riser Drainage Ditch runs straight through these blocks. Housing is mostly one- and two-storey frame dwellings with a few concrete-block garages, a printing shop with an electric motor on Niehaus Avenue and a bakery near Liberty and Washington. Little Ferry Public School No. 2 stands on the west side of Liberty Street. The business corner at Liberty and Washington Avenue has stores, a bowling and motion picture hall and A. Holz's hotel, meeting rooms and bowling alleys, and the Pearl Button Factory stands on Liberty near Eckel Road. St. Margaret's Roman Catholic Church faces Washington Avenue. In the east, Kavrik Street leads to Marschall Avenue past John and Joseph Streets, and a newer grid of Slate, Katherine, John and Helen Streets is laid out in largely empty lots; Hester and Nicholas Streets run south to Warren Street. Large undeveloped tracts (blocks 47 and 54) take up much of the sheet; the ground beyond the borough limits in the south-west is left blank with a reference to the Garfield volume.
notes: John Street east of Helen (the east-west street) is now Chamberlain Avenue; the north-south John Street off Kavrik keeps its name.
Marschall Avenue is now Marshall Avenue.
Nicholas Avenue is now Nicholas Street.
Little Ferry Public School No. 2, St. Margaret's R.C. Church, A. Holz hotel and bowling alleys, and the Pearl Button Factory are on this sheet.
Helen Street was left out of the fit: both its junctions were 4 to 5 m off, a sign that the modern street is not on the old line.
Liberty Street / Niehaus Avenue was rejected by the fit (8.6 m).
Liberty Street is drawn about 32 ft wide against a modern right-of-way of about 50 ft.
The Moonachie side of the borough line is left blank: 'Borough of Moonachie, see Garfield Volume'.

Map, 100 ft. Centre of the borough: Liberty, Niehaus Av, Union Av, Henry, Christina, Sabina, Charles, Jackson, William, Kavrik, John, Joseph, Marschall (now Marshall Avenue), Katherine, Slate, Helen, John (east-west, now Chamberlain Avenue), Washington Av, Lorena, Hester, Nicholas, Mehrhof Rd, Warren. One part.

sheet-3.description: The north-western part of Little Ferry at 100 ft to an inch, where the borough meets Lodi Township. Lodi Avenue crosses the top of the sheet diagonally from the north-west to Liberty Street, with the Lodi Township boundary drawn along its centre and the borough limits following the line of a drainage ditch north of it. Off Lodi Avenue run Franklin Street (a 20 ft street bending south-west), Wilson Street, Monnett Street and Paroubek Street; a second, east-west Franklin Street crosses Paroubek further south. Red Neck Avenue runs from St. John Street in the south-west to Liberty Street, crossed by Charles and Jackson Streets, and William Street runs along the southern edge. The Riser Ditch winds south through the eastern blocks. Most of the western half is large unbuilt tracts (blocks 35 and 36) with scattered dwellings along Franklin, Ann and St. John Streets. Building is densest along Paroubek Street and Red Neck Avenue: frame dwellings, a stone-fronted store, and the button factory of John Dvorak & Sons on Paroubek Street, with a second small button factory on Lodi Avenue. At the junction of Red Neck Avenue and Liberty Street are a contractors' yard and a storage building, and a short stub of Heuer Street leads east to sheet 4. Liberty Street runs north to south along the eastern edge, with a row of dwellings at its northern end and a fire alarm box at Lodi Avenue.
notes: Lodi Avenue is now Main Street east of Paroubek Street and Lodi Street west of it.
The east-west Franklin Street crossing Paroubek Street is now Garfield Street; the diagonal Franklin Street keeps its name.
Red Neck Avenue is now Redneck Avenue.
Charles Street south of Red Neck Avenue is now Roosevelt Street.
The Lodi Township boundary runs along the centre of Lodi Avenue.
Button factory of John Dvorak & Sons on Paroubek Street.

Modern Franklin Street lies about 20 m north-west of the drawn one; its junction with Lodi Street was not used. Redneck Avenue / Saint John Street was hand-picked and sits about 10 m off a fit to the eastern points, so the western third of the sheet is less certain.

Map, 100 ft. North-west: Lodi Av (now Main Street east and Lodi Street west of Paroubek), Franklin, Ann, St. John, Wilson, Monnett, Paroubek, Franklin (lower, east-west; now Garfield Street), Red Neck Av (Redneck Avenue), Charles (south of Red Neck; now Roosevelt Street), Jackson, William, Liberty, Heuer. Lodi Township line along Lodi Av. One part.

sheet-4.description: The densest part of Little Ferry at 100 ft to an inch, centred on Lodi Avenue, which crosses the sheet from Liberty Street in the north-west towards Bergen Turnpike in the east. North of Lodi Avenue a grid of long narrow blocks runs up Charles, Garden, Brandt and Grand Streets, closely built with one- and two-storey frame dwellings, some brick-cased, and a few concrete-block garages; Kaufman Avenue is laid out in vacant lots in the north-east. Lodi Avenue is the business street: stores, Zglozynski's Hotel near Liberty Street, the T. J. Sokol Hall on Garden Street, the Evangelical Congregational Church, a button factory behind it, a large garage for 18 cars, and the Little Ferry Hook and Ladder Co. No. 1 with an alarm box. South of Lodi Avenue are Heuer Street, Anna and Center Streets, Grove Street and Schulz Place, with John and Joseph Streets running down to Kavrik Street and William Street along the south-west. A large block of truck gardens (block 24) lies between Center and Pickens Streets. In the south, Marschall Avenue runs diagonally past Beech and Maple Streets with an auto repair shop and, at its lower end, the Fire Department house of Hose Co. No. 1. Liberty Street bounds the sheet on the west and Pickens Street on the east; the southern third is largely empty ground belonging to sheet 2.
notes: Lodi Avenue is now Main Street.
Anna Street is now the northern part of Marshall Avenue; Marschall Avenue is now Marshall Avenue.
Brandt Street is now Brant Street.
Schulz Place is now part of Maple Street.
Zglozynski's Hotel, the T. J. Sokol Hall, the Evangelical Congregational Church, Little Ferry Hook and Ladder Co. No. 1 and the Fire Department (Hose Co. No. 1) house are on this sheet.
Modern Frederick Street, Werneking Place, Park Avenue, Vogt Lane and Sylvan Avenue cross ground that is blocks or truck gardens on the sheet; they were not used.

Map, 100 ft. North-centre: Lodi Av (Main Street), Liberty, Charles, Garden, Brandt (Brant Street), Grand, Heuer, John, Joseph, Kavrik, Anna (now part of Marshall Avenue), Marschall Av, Center, Grove, Beech, Maple, Schulz Pl, Pickens, Kaufman Av. One part.

sheet-5.description: The north-eastern part of Little Ferry at 100 ft to an inch, along Bergen Turnpike down to the Hackensack River. The turnpike runs north-south through the middle of the sheet, then bends south-east past the Nine Mile House to a 170 ft steel drawbridge over the river. West of it, Kaufman Avenue and Lodi Avenue run in from the west, both laid out in long narrow lots; Kaufman Avenue carries a row of frame dwellings and Lodi Avenue the Wilson Public School No. 1, a printing shop and a few houses, with a bank in a triangular building where Lodi Avenue meets the turnpike. Pickens Street forms the western edge, with stubs of Grove Street and Schulz Place. South of Lodi Avenue a large open block (25) holds a pond that dries in summer and the Henry Gardner brick works, with drying racks, a mixing pit and a long kiln shed with temporary burning kilns, bunk houses and dwellings beside Riverside Avenue and Washington Avenue; stubs of Treptow and Ludwig Streets lead south to sheet 6. East of the turnpike stand the Hermann Walker Realty Co. and Walker Cement Products works with a drying shed. Along the turnpike near the river are a garage for 12 cars, a post office, a lunch wagon, a service station, stores and the Nine Mile House with its bowling alley, pavilion and stage. The east of the sheet is open meadow cut by two tidal creeks running into the Hackensack River.
notes: Lodi Avenue is now Main Street.
Riverside Avenue between Washington Avenue and Bergen Turnpike is now part of Washington Avenue.
Wilson Public School No. 1, the Henry Gardner brick works, Walker Cement Products and the Nine Mile House are on this sheet.

The Bergen Turnpike / Lodi Avenue junction lies in a bend of the turnpike beside a triangular building and was not used. A hand-picked Bergen Turnpike / Kaufman Avenue point disagreed with the other five by about 30 m (the turnpike stretch between Kaufman and Lodi Avenues measures about 10 percent short of the modern one) and was removed.

Placed from five junctions on Washington Avenue and Pickens Street only, at its own fitted scale (3.99 px/ft, held with scale_ft 98.7); the turnpike and river front in the east have no control and may be off by 10 m or more.

Map, 100 ft. North-east: Bergen Turnpike, Kaufman Av, Lodi Av, Pickens, Washington Av, Riverside Av (north of Washington now part of Washington Avenue), Henry Gardner brick works, Walker cement products, Nine Mile House and the Hackensack River drawbridge. One part.

sheet-6.description: The south-eastern part of Little Ferry at 100 ft to an inch, from Washington Avenue south to the brick yards on the Hackensack River. Washington Avenue crosses the top of the sheet from Mehrhof Road and bends south-east to Riverside Avenue near the river. North of it, between Marschall Avenue, Maple Street, Schulz Place and Pickens Street, is the village centre: a drug store, groceries and stores, a sausage factory and slaughter house, the Carl Becker hall, hotel and bowling alleys with a stage hall, the Little Ferry Hotel, the Lincoln & Ulmer cigar factory and a plumber's shop. East of Pickens Street a small grid on Treptow, Ludwig and Riverside Streets carries frame dwellings and a hall. Mehrhof Road runs down the western edge with dwellings along it and short streets leading off it: an unnamed street, Warren Street, Henches Place, Coomann Street, Hartwick Street with a small factory, Columbus Avenue, and in the south-west Lafayette, Lincoln and Dietrich Streets with the L. Heinige button factory and the head of Maiden Lane. The middle of the sheet is open ground (block 59). In the south-east are the General Electric Co. Edison Lamp Works chemical plant, with tungsten furnace room, ore plant, mill, laboratory and electrolyzer plant, and the N. Mehrhof Co. upper brick yard, with clay banks and a drained clay pit, mixing and machine sheds, sleeping rooms, a drying yard and a long up-draught brick kiln burning shed on the Hackensack River with a shipping dock.
notes: Marschall Avenue is now Marshall Avenue; Schulz Place is now part of Maple Street; Coomann Street is now Prospect Avenue.
General Electric Co. Edison Lamp Works (chemical plant) and the N. Mehrhof Co. upper brick yard are on this sheet.
Carl Becker hall, hotel and bowling alleys, the Little Ferry Hotel and the Lincoln & Ulmer cigar factory face Washington Avenue.
An unnamed short street east of Mehrhof Road is lettered only 'Street'.
Dietrich Street / Mehrhof Road was hand-picked: the detector paired a block line about 50 ft north of the street; the hand-picked junction agrees with the modern node to within 1 m.
Riverside Avenue / Washington Avenue was hand-picked and agrees with the fit to 0.4 m.

Map, 100 ft. South-east: Washington Av, Marschall Av, Maple, Schulz Pl, Pickens, Treptow, Ludwig, Riverside Av, Mehrhof Rd with Warren, Henches, Coomann, Hartwick, Columbus, Lafayette, Lincoln, Dietrich; General Electric Edison Lamp Works and N. Mehrhof Co. upper brick yard on the Hackensack River. One part.

sheet-7-1.description: The main part of sheet 7, at 100 ft to an inch with north up, covering the southern tip of Little Ferry below sheet 6. In the north-west, Mehrhof Road runs south from Dietrich Street, and Maiden Lane runs parallel to it to the east; the block between them (64) is built with frame dwellings and a hen house, with numbered lots facing Dietrich Street and Maiden Lane. West of Mehrhof Road is a large open tract (block 80). A winding creek runs south through the middle of the part towards the Hackensack River. The rest of the part is the M. Mehrhof Co. Inc. lower brick yard (block 66): a drained clay pit with clay banks, a suction pipe and a frame house for draining the pits, an open flume, the office and scale, boarding houses, storage buildings, two long rows of mixing sheds with machine sheds on an elevated shaft and power line, drying yards, a driveway, and a long up-draught brick kiln burning shed, 250 ft long, beside a slip off the Hackensack River. The note gives a capacity of 10 million bricks a year, with work in the summer months only. In the north-east corner, above the heavy dividing line, the sheet repeats the end of the M. Mehrhof & Co. upper yard from sheet 6: a boarding house and an up-draught kiln burning shed beside the river.
notes: M. Mehrhof Co. Inc. lower brick yard; the upper yard continues from sheet 6 (the sheet refers to sheet 6 for its report).

Placed from two detected junctions on Dietrich Street and a derived point on Mehrhof Road (drawn direction, modern bearing, assumed scale); the south of the part, the brick yard, has no control of its own.

Map, 100 ft, two parts divided by a heavy line. Part 1 (main, north up): Mehrhof Rd, Dietrich, Maiden Lane and the M. Mehrhof Co. lower brick yard, with the end of the upper yard top right. Part 2 (inset at the right, turned about 60 degrees, own north arrow): Bergen Turnpike at the City of Hackensack line with Backel Av (now Backiel Street) and the Hackensack Brick Co.

sheet-7-2.description: An inset on the right of sheet 7, separated from the main part by a heavy line and drawn at 100 ft to an inch but turned about 60 degrees, with its own north arrow. It shows the northern end of Little Ferry where Bergen Turnpike reaches the City of Hackensack line. Backel Avenue runs off the turnpike to the west, lined with a few frame dwellings and a store, and dwellings face the turnpike itself; a 20-inch water pipe runs along it, and the borough limit with the City of Hackensack crosses the turnpike diagonally. Ponds, an old clay pit and a winding tidal creek lie south of the turnpike. A lane runs from the turnpike to the Hackensack Brick Co., which occupies the rest of the inset between a pond and the Hackensack River: a mixing shed with an electric motor, a drying yard, a bunk house, dwellings, a pump house for draining the pit, a large clay pit, frame drying racks, a brick machine and dumping platform, and two burning sheds without permanent kilns. The note says there is no watchman, power and lights are electric and there is no fire apparatus.
notes: Backel Avenue is now Backiel Street.
The lane to the Hackensack Brick Co. has no modern counterpart in the OpenStreetMap extract.
The inset's north arrow points about 45 degrees from the top of the page, but the turnpike and Backel Avenue give about 63 to 68 degrees against their modern bearings; the arrow was not used.
Anchored on the single junction Bergen Turnpike / Backiel Street with assumed scale; rotation from the drawn street lines.

Map, 100 ft, two parts divided by a heavy line. Part 1 (main, north up): Mehrhof Rd, Dietrich, Maiden Lane and the M. Mehrhof Co. lower brick yard, with the end of the upper yard top right. Part 2 (inset at the right, turned about 60 degrees, own north arrow): Bergen Turnpike at the City of Hackensack line with Backel Av (now Backiel Street) and the Hackensack Brick Co.
